And I pointed out that -- more or less what would he have expected when, in reality, he could have been claiming that he was being attacked and looking for assistance and all he did do was grab 20 policemen from different countries all over the world and turned the media against him.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. McElligott. If I could just interrupt there, and -- because this incident is described in your statement as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: And I would ask if we could tender this document, this video 4809.9.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Just to make another point on the tape. He did mention that we expressed gratitude for feeding them and -- or feeding his people, our people, and for the help they got. The fact that they had to feed them meant that they were not free -- our people couldn't get their own meals, but we did express our gratitude and I did do so to Mr. Martinovic and to Mr. Spanovic, and I did that publicly and openly to them. Because they did contribute in a positive way to achieving the end result, and I would still say thank you for that. At the same time, I did find out that they'd breached the Vance Plan, it was not part of the planning, we were meant to have a freedom of movement, and we were quite firm on that too.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: So we would again tender that video 4809.9.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P2174, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thanks.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: Could we now look to document 5177 in your binder.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: And if we could get that on the monitor as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: This is a sitrep from Sector East. Now, if we look on the first page of this document, there's a list of addressees, down the left side. What do the terms FC and DFC stand for in that list of addresses?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD McELLIGOTT
utterances.text: The Force Commander and the Deputy Force Commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: Now if we turn over to page 2.3, and sub-point 3, and this is the second paragraph from the bottom. It states that an UNCIVPOL vehicle was stopped at the Batina bridge. Are you aware of UNCIVPOL vehicles being stopped?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD McELLIGOTT
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours. Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: Looking at the last line at the bottom of the same page, it refers to terrorisation of the non-Serb population continuing and it says to see the details in CIVPOL reports. Why would this UNPROFOR sitrep refer to the CIVPOL reports?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD McELLIGOTT
utterances.text: There was a close liaison between all the elements in the mission. You had the military component, you had the civil affairs, and CIVPOL, and there was a close relationship so that it is clearly obvious that there was a meeting, they were familiar with incidents that we had encountered, and they were bringing that to the notice of the Force Commander from the military perspective. They were reporting to the person in charge in the HQ.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: We tender this document, 5177, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P2175.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: Mr. McElligott, I'm now going to address some documents that concern the issue of shelling which is referred to your statement at paragraph 148. But these are different documents. The first one is 1608. And while you're getting to that, I'll ask you: Firstly, what impact did the shelling have on the work of the UNCIVPOL monitors?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD McELLIGOTT
utterances.text: The impact was it immediately presented a danger to their own persons in the sense that they were working out in the field along -- all over the mission area so they were exposed to that risk of being struck. That was an immediate risk. But there was also the -- the fallout effect that when shelling occurred, they were unable to engage in their patrols into the communities and do their job. And, again, while you have Croatian side shelling the sector, the reality was that our monitors couldn't get to visit their own -- their people. So in the sense, they were almost impeding our duty in respect of engaging -- of minding the people they wanted us to mind.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: Looking to the front page of this document, do you recognise the signature of who it's from?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD McELLIGOTT
utterances.text: It's Yolanda Auger. She was the deputy to Cedric Thornberry at the UN head -- civil affairs headquarters.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: And then if we look over the page and we look at page 2, what type of document is this?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD McELLIGOTT
utterances.text: Again, it's a -- what I would call a protest letter written by Cedric Thornberry, who was the director of civil affairs.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: Your Honour, we tender this document, 1608.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P2176.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: Sir, if you could now look to document 1616. And this is an UNPROFOR coded cable and it's again addressing the issue of shelling of civilian targets. If we look at the first page of addressees, who was this sent to?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD McELLIGOTT
utterances.text: This goes to Mr. Annan at UN headquarters in New York.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: If we skip right to the end page, and for you this should be the page ending 7738. In e-court it's page 3. We can see who the underlying report was provided by at the end there.

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD McELLIGOTT
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: Who -- who is that?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD McELLIGOTT
utterances.text: Clements, he's the lieutenant-colonel. He's in charge of the -- commanding officer of the UNMOs, the United Nations Military Observers.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: Thank you. And I would ask you again to speak slowly and clearly for the purposes of the transcript. Now who were the UNMOs and how did their work relate to the work of the UNCIVPOL monitors?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD McELLIGOTT
utterances.text: The UNMOs were -- they were a group of military observers, they were unarmed, and in general they were acting as liaison persons between the -- both sides on the front line would be -- they were the facilitators when conflict arose on the front line. And shelling would be an obvious one where they would engage in talks and try and stabilise the situation again. So they played a key role in that area. They were the first-response team from the UN on the ground and they were amenable to all sides and available to all sides.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: We tender document 1616.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P2177.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: Looking now to document 5204. Now, while this is coming up, I noticed in paragraph 81 of your statement you refer to P.J. McGowan as the head of operations at UNCIVPOL HQ. So does that mean that you took over when you started as head of operations at UNCIVPOL from McGowan; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD McELLIGOTT
utterances.text: That is correct, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: If we look at this document on page 1, do you recognise the signature?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD McELLIGOTT
utterances.text: Yes, that is P.J. McGowan's signature.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: Now if we go to page 5, which is ending 5874, the ERN number. And if we look at point 8 there, the report states that: "There will be public meetings with government -- local government in an effort to prevent criminality." Are you aware of meetings of this nature?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD McELLIGOTT
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours. Meetings were held within the sectors. Meetings were held with the police on, I would say, regular enough occasions and very often weekly, and I would say at station level, some of our monitors would go there every day. Then you have what would appear to be a community-type meeting here, which has an agenda -- I suppose there's an information element attached to it of informing the community of what is happening. And there's an issue about the exploration of fuel -- of a fuel situation. There's --

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: That's okay. [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD McELLIGOTT
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ... it's a very open type of agenda for a community meeting. And it's a type of one where you could see it as perhaps a first engagement with a group. Where you're going -- I'm going to go on and engage to more focussed issues of concern.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: If we then look to the attached report which is referred to at the end of this page, so the following page, which should end 5875. You'll see that this is a report on an incident of violent intimidation by an individual called Djoko Briga. And it describes how Johansen, Larry Moore and someone called Gerard Sexton go to the Dalj police station to follow up on this.

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD McELLIGOTT
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: Now, firstly, you've mentioned Johansen and Larry Moore. Did you know Gerard Sexton?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD McELLIGOTT
utterances.text: Yes, I do. He was an Irish police monitor on the mission.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: And would it be normal for the commissioner to personally go to the police station to follow up on an incident?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD McELLIGOTT
utterances.text: I expect or I suspect that he was actually in the mission area at that particular time, visiting the area, and having reviewed the situation decided to go, and indeed I think did Mrs. Naga attend as well, if I'm not clear on that one. But, yes, he is -- he did go. It wouldn't have been normal for him to go. The monitors would deal with the issues themselves at local level.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: I see that in the middle of the page before us, and this should be the page ending 5785, there's a quote from Djoko Briga, saying: "I will be beat you up again in front of the militia and CIVPOL." Did you hear of threats like that being made to a CIVPOL representative?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD McELLIGOTT
utterances.text: Could you repeat the question here?

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: Certainly. There is a quote from the suspect Djoko Briga stating -- he is report as stating: "I will beat you up again in front of the militia and CIVPOL." Did you hear of threats like that being made to CIVPOL monitors?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD McELLIGOTT
utterances.text: Well, that's a very specific threat. I can't recall off the top of my head where you have a culprit literally dictating the agenda blatantly and violent -- almost violently as to how he will respond -- it -- to a matter, so off the top of my head I can't say I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: If we look further down, at the second-last sentence of this page, it says: "Briga is employed by the town council in Dalj and responsible for the housing section." What impact would it have on victims where individuals like this were involved in crimes?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD McELLIGOTT
utterances.text: I think if you go back to the very beginning of the report where the initial threat was made it highlights the -- the motive for the -- the -- the initial crime. And ... he called -- the -- Djoko Briga called to his home with unidentified men and told him to leave Dalj. Djoko Briga told him that if he and his family were not gone by the next day, or the next morning, they would be killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD McELLIGOTT
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ... and what you then have -- --

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: Sorry, from your review of that, what is the motive for the crime?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD McELLIGOTT
utterances.text: The motive is that he wants him out of his house, and obviously if he is involved in the town council housing section he has other clients in mind to be housed. And when you look at the fact that he was being dealt with by the police, he was blatantly challenging them and more or less telling them that he didn't give a damn what they did.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: We tender 5204, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Gosnell.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: We object to that. There's no foundation given what the witness has testified to. The witness appears to have no direct knowledge of this event, wasn't asked any questions whether he had any direct knowledge or memory of this event. What he did do was he identified that that was Mr. McGowan's signature. He confirmed that community meetings, police meetings were held. He confirms he knows Gerry Sexton. He was then asked a hypothetical question about what impact this crime would have and then he speculated about the motive. And then he gave two indications that were negative to the contents of the document. One was that he said it was not normal that the author would have gone to the police station. And he said he had no knowledge of any other specific threats of the type that are indicated in this second page of this document, of the second document. So you'll know, Your Honours, we've made a submission in respect of foundation with witnesses, and I think this is a good example of absence of foundation for the admission of this document with this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Gillett.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: Yeah, indeed, the document is of a format similar to many documents reviewed by the witness. He's identified the individuals involved in the incident and in creating the document, he's, as my learned friend has observed, added additional comments about local meetings with local government and he has added context to the events described in this document. Now, the fact that he says that it would not be normal for a police commissioner to go along, although it is a negative answer it provides relevant context when you're reading and understanding this document. So we say that there is a sufficient foundation for the admission of this document and that additional issues can, of course, be raised in cross-examination and can go to the weight placed on this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Gosnell.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Well, Mr. President, that's exactly the problem. There isn't really anything to be gone into on cross-examination because the witness doesn't know anything about the core allegation contained in the attachment. What can be gone into on cross-examination? Nothing. And that's the -- that's the core reason, I suggest, as to why this document is being tendered, and it's that content that cannot be cross-examined on.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: Well, again, that would go to weight. If the Defence chooses to cross-examine on additional aspects, we do not understand the witness to have to talk about every aspect of a document but we maintain that he has talked about significant aspects in relation to this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Gillett, when you said that the witness identified individuals involved in the incident --

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: I should --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: -- who are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: I should have clarified that he said -- he stated that he knew Johansen and Larry Moore as UNCIVPOL monitors, and Gerard Sexton, he explained who he was. So when I refer to the incident, I refer to the description of them going and speaking to this individual.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: The objection is sustained. Please continue, Mr. Gillett.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: Thank you. If we now turn to -- if we could now play a video, which is 4848.1. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: If we pause there before we start playing, do you recognise any of the individuals shown there?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD McELLIGOTT
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours. The lady at the microphones is Jeannie Peterson. I referred to her earlier as the head of civil affairs in Sector South.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: And could you describe what she is wearing or how she appears?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD McELLIGOTT
utterances.text: In what sense?

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: To identify which of the two women she is?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD McELLIGOTT
utterances.text: She is the lady -- the person in the middle and to the right of the person dressed in a UN uniform.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: If we could now play the video.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] "... assistance, especially for the derivatives in medicines. Today the motorway Belgrade-Zagreb will be opened. Jeannie Peterson, chief for civil affairs of the UNPROFOR, said the same. At the press conference in Belgrade, the representative of UNPROFOR, Jeannie Peterson, head of UNPROFOR civilian affairs, said that from Belgrade to Zagreb a journey will be organised along the motorway. This highway will be used for transportation of civilians for the first time since 1991. This UNPROFOR action will represent demonstration of goodwill and two groups will meet in Okucani where a press conference will be organised. Talking about the situation in protected areas, Jeannie Peterson said that it was gradually improving in the majority of sectors in the light of progress of the Geneva negotiating progress. Violations of the cease-fire on part of the Croats are fewer and the Serbs have better co-operation with the UNPROFOR. However, in Sector East in Baranja, Serb paramilitaries continued to carry out terrorist attacks and local police is not doing anything to stop this. Arson, looting and destruction of houses persist in Sector Sot, and according to Ms. Peterson, the Serb side is responsible for most of those."

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: Mr. McElligott --

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: Apologies. There appears to be an issue with my microphone. Am I coming through loud and clear?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: Am I coming through now? I believe there's a microphone on in the booth. Am I coming through now? Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Yeah, it's okay now.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: Mr. McElligott, in the video we've seen just, Jeannie Peterson says that in Sector East in Baranja, Serb paramilitaries continue to carry out terrorist acts and the local police doesn't do anything about it. Which paramilitary groups operated in Sector East?

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Mr. President, I object. Let's consider what was just put to the witness. We actually don't have Jeannie Peterson's words on the audiotape. We have a broadcaster, from wherever the origin of this broadcast is, summarising her words. Those words have now been put in front of the witness and then the question being asked by my learned friend was whether paramilitary groups or which paramilitary groups operated in Sector East. Now, it certainly seems leading even though the -- even though the -- the video didn't actually specifically name paramilitary groups. So I'm not really -- I -- I would suggest and my objection is it's poor leading but it's nevertheless leading, and the Prosecution has previously quite correctly said that it's not proper to put a video to a witness first because that is leading the witness to a certain conclusion. Better to ask the question, have an answer. If there's a lack of memory, then whatever material is to be put to the witness, can be put to the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Basically I agree with you, Mr. Gosnell. But what is the -- besides -- consequence in your -- in your view. Should we -- should we not allow OTP to ask whether the witness knows about paramilitaries in the sector?

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: Your Honours, if I could -- sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: I -- I think -- I think I would rather have a reaction of Mr. Gosnell first, Mr. Gillett.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Well, I -- I think I would ask the Prosecution to move on to the next question. Because I -- I would suggest we're coming to something leading. And -- it's already -- the seed of the leading has already been planted and we can't see yet what the prejudice is going to be. So, yes, indeed, I would say that the remedy is ask the Prosecution to go to the next question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Gillett.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: Thank you for your patience. We don't understand there to be a general rule that videos which are narrated over the top cannot be used with witnesses. And in this specific instance we're dealing with a Rule 92 ter witness who does have mentions of paramilitaries in his statement. So the difficulty that we face in these situations is that there are references in the evidence that's already admitted of the witness and we don't want to repeat all of that evidence but we do want to try and elicit additional details if they're available. And this is a parallel situation where we have an exhibit which mentioned some detail but doesn't mention which paramilitary groups, and I'm trying to elicit that additional detail from the witness should he know it. So that's the basis on which we present this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Could you direct me to a specific paragraph or -- or paragraphs in the statement? The witness's statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: Sure. Sure. Your Honours, for instance, we have in paragraph 123 of the statement a Sector East military situation report, which refers to the JNA's failure to disarm paramilitary troops. So, again, there's reference in the same area, Sector East, to paramilitary troops which is provided in the video.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: The objection is overruled. Please proceed, Mr. Gillett.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: Mr. McElligott, I'll repeat my question. In the clip we've seen, Jeannie Peterson is reported as saying that in Sector East in Baranja, Serb paramilitaries continue to carry out terrorist attacks and the local police doesn't do anything about it. Which paramilitary groups operated in Sector East?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD McELLIGOTT
utterances.text: I have referred to the -- in the -- what I call the special police earlier on in my evidence. They would be one group. I wouldn't define them as a paramilitary group in that sense. But Arkan and his people were also in Sector East, and I have referred to them in those terms elsewhere in my statement. So I would be conscious of they being there. I'm also conscious of the fact that the police themselves have declared that when people of this nature are engaged in activities, that it is beyond them to deal with it. In other words, that there is another overseeing power beyond their authority. And it is in that context I see the police problem. Refusing to deal with it might be -- mightn't exactly be correct. I think being capable or being -- having the capacity to do -- or the scope to do it and the freedom to do it would be perhaps getting closer to where the issue -- the real issue lies. And they have confided, indeed I have met officers myself who told me that they had a difficulty, and indeed I think there are several reports there alluding to that fact as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: You've used the term "another overseeing power beyond their authority." Can you clarify that at all?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD McELLIGOTT
utterances.text: You have the police functioning as a police force and at station or opstina level they have a role, and their line of command, as I would see it, to the ultimate height is Milan Martic. Now side by side with that you have the special police and who controlled them in between, I have no idea. And I don't -- and I'm not sure if others know. But there was -- the police certainly sensed and told us that they were in a vacuum when they engaged in unlawful activity.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: Now, Peterson in the clip that we've seen also refers to arson, looting, and destruction of houses in Sector South and she says that the Serb side is responsible for most of these crimes. How does that compare with your experience with Sector South?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD McELLIGOTT
utterances.text: Sector South has many, many crimes recorded against the minority Croatian population and again they -- again you take where your suspects are seen at the crime scenes. They are men in militia uniform, in military uniform, and I would say that they are Serbians attacking the Croatian people.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: Your Honours, we would tender this video 4848.1.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Mr. President, we object. We don't often object to commentaries being provided by the media or the news -- a news reporter. But in this case it's being presented as if it was the words of Ms. Peterson, whereas in fact it's a -- it's someone else saying what those words were, without knowing who that someone else is. I think in this context, there's not a -- this is one situation where it's not sufficiently reliable to be admitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: To clarify, is the Defence disputing that this media conference took place and Jeannie Peterson gave this conference, or are they simply disputing the fact that it is reporting of her words rather than her words?

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Mr. President, it is often that there are three people sitting at a desk and saying something. So that is not in dispute. What is in dispute is the nature of what she said, which then was the foundation for some remarks. But what she said cannot be reliably -- we say cannot be reliably inferred based on an anonymous commentary by a media reporter. And that's the problem. That's why it is not admissible.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: Your Honours, perhaps if I could clarify to say the -- in light of the witness's comments in relation to this, if we rely on this video for the purpose not of her specific words, not of precisely what she was stating, but in terms of the fact a media conference was held where these issues were raised, and then the witness has provided his additional comments in relation to these issues and he has identified the speaker as well as Jeannie Peterson.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: I was going to ask Mr. Gosnell that given the jurisprudence of the Tribunal in terms of hearsay evidence, since we are not in a pure common law courtroom, could you expand on why the -- what you say is the commentary is distinct from the very words -- ought not to be admitted?

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Well, Judge Hall, you're quite right and my understanding of the jurisprudence is that hearsay is not inadmissible. That doesn't necessarily mean that hearsay always is admissible. And in this case we have no indication as to who is giving this hearsay information about what Ms. Peterson said, and normally, anonymous hearsay actually is one of those categories where often Trial Chambers will say: We cannot accord that any weight whatsoever. And if you apply that reasoning to the admissibility standards is -- if you know, Your Honours, that you cannot rely on anonymous hearsay at the end of the day, then there is no reason to admit this information. Now, if the Prosecution wishes to tender the video without the commentary, there would be no objection to that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Gillett, do we know where the broadcast comes from? Who -- who was broadcasting this? And I -- I --

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: Your Honours, perhaps I could look into that and come back to this. We understand it is Serbian news television, but I don't have all the details right at my fingertips. So perhaps I could come back with those details.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: All right. All right. Please proceed. We'll wait --

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: Thank you --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: -- until we have that information.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: Mr. McElligott, if we could now look at document 5293. And this is a document concerning mass graves. And I note in your statement at paragraph 132, you refer to a report that you forwarded to the police commissioner concerning the Ovcara mass grave. So before we look at this document 5293, I'd first ask you why was it that you forwarded a report to the police commissioner about this mass grave?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD McELLIGOTT
utterances.text: I -- that would my normal line of command in forwarding material from CIVPOL, say, to civil affairs or to the Force Commander or to some other source at a higher level. So he would be the signing authority when it is leaving CIVPOL to go to some other department such as civil affairs or the military.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: I would ask you to speak very clearly into the microphones, please. If we now look at document 5293, do you have that there?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD McELLIGOTT
utterances.text: I think it's coming up, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: Now, this is a report. And if we look at page 1, the front page, do you recognise the signature on this?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD McELLIGOTT
utterances.text: Yes. It's Kjell Johansen's, the CIVPOL commissioner's.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: Then if we look at the page overleaf, at the bottom of that, do you recognise the signature there?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD McELLIGOTT
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours. It's Larry Moore.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: On the same page that you're looking at, there's a third long paragraph that says that local president Milan Ilic would not authorise an exhumation and that there should be no investigations of events prior to the formation of the RSK. Do you recall that reason being given in relation to investigations of the Ovcara mass grave, which you refer to in your statement?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD McELLIGOTT
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: The attached report to this, this document, says on the last page, and this should end 3821, right at the end, the last sentence, I believe says: "There's a concern that the RSK authorities would tie exhumation to other issues." That's right at the end.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: 3821. Yes, correct. Right at the end.

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD McELLIGOTT
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: Where it says there was a concern they would tie the exhumation to other issues, what is this referring to?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD McELLIGOTT
utterances.text: At the time I understand there were calls to open mass graves in -- on the other side, on the Croatian side as well, that there would be a joint approach to opening mass graves.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: Your Honours, we tender 5293 into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P2178, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: If we now look across to 5228. And this is an UNPROFOR military info summary from August 1992. In your statement, you authenticate similar military info reports. For example, at paragraph 129. Now, if you have that there, if you look at the addressees, would UNCIVPOL have received this report?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD McELLIGOTT
utterances.text: It's listed as one of the recipients or departments to have it circulated to.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: If we then look to page 4, which should be ending 8506, 8506, and point 4 on this page. Here it states that a militia leader, Mr. Vranic, in Baranja, has ordered his men to carry rifles. If you see that --

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD McELLIGOTT
utterances.text: Yes, I have it -- [overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: Can you tell us whether that order would be in accordance with the Vance Plan?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD McELLIGOTT
utterances.text: No, Your Honours. The Vance Plan stated that the police were to be armed with side-arms only.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: If we then look to the following page, which should end 8507, at the top, it states that in Sector South some minor demobilisation took place but that mostly TDF soldiers changed uniform into special militia or the uniform of the Krajina Knin Corps. Were you aware of this changing of uniforms?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD McELLIGOTT
utterances.text: Yes, we received reports from our own monitors, and indeed there is one documented here where a monitor reports seeing people wearing different uniforms today and that report would be coming on the basis that they know the people and they are now wearing a different uniform. So it was a question of they knew the people on the ground and they now see them wearing a different uniform and they interchanged uniforms from time to time.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: If we look at page 9, which should be two pages over, and point 1. Do you see problems there with the Red Berets?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD McELLIGOTT
utterances.text: Which -- which page are you on?

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: Page 9. It should be page 8511.

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD McELLIGOTT
utterances.text: I have different ...

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: Do you see a point 1 there? It may be 8510. It may be the preceding page?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD McELLIGOTT
utterances.text: Yeah, I think we're on different page numbers. What date is it recorded as?

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: If you give me a moment, I'll just check.

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD McELLIGOTT
utterances.text: I think we're on different page numbers.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: Indeed, it's the page that should end 8511, at the top. And do you see that under 19th August, 1992, point number 1.

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD McELLIGOTT
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: It says: "The increasing militance of the Red Berets is a continuing concern in Sector East. They are based in Bapska and they refuse to deal with UNCIVPOL, claiming they are military in nature." Now, firstly, was there supposed to be military units in Sector East at this stage?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD McELLIGOTT
utterances.text: No, Your Honours. Demilitarisation was meant to take place from the outset of the mission. That -- in fact that was the basis of the mission. And they should not be there. And, secondly, the whole core of the -- advancing the mission was openness, interchange, co-operation, and you can see where it's being refused here, and they are indeed just not accounting for themselves.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: Your Honours, we would tender this document, 5228.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P2179.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: If we could now look to document 1322. This is, again, an UNPROFOR military info report. It's 1322. And this military info report is a week later, five days later than a similar military info report which is authenticated in your statement.

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD McELLIGOTT
utterances.text: I don't seem to have 13 --

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD McELLIGOTT
utterances.text: Is it at the rear?

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: It should be in the second group of documents.

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD McELLIGOTT
utterances.text: Okay. Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: You have it there?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD McELLIGOTT
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: Now, firstly if we look at page 1, again, it lists UNCIVPOL as an addressee. But if we skip across two pages to the one that should end 1933 at the top. This is also page 2 of 17, it's called. So if you look at point 3(E) on this page there's a heading: "Capabilities and possible intentions Sector East." And it says: "A.J. is ready to enter the sector in case of return of Croatian refugees." Are you aware what they're describing in that sentence?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD McELLIGOTT
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. There was a proposal, I suppose, it was a bit more stronger than that, that there was going to be an incursion of civilians into the UNPA for the purpose of returning to their homes. A mass entry of civilians into the mission area. And this was initiated by the Croatian side. And this is indicating a response on -- from the Serbian side in the event of that case, or actually planning for it.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: And was this a concern to UNPROFOR and UNCIVPOL?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD McELLIGOTT
utterances.text: Yes, it was. Again, it was a heightening of tensions. I suppose in reality the circumstances weren't right for their return. We were still very much in conflict and the first step of the Vance Plan had not been taken even. So it did heighten the tensions. And you were leading into serious conflict. It was going to involve civilians. So it was a serious issue of concern to the UN mission as to how you handle a situation like that. But, again, the approach in those situations would have been one of negotiating and trying to negotiate [indiscernible]. So you had confrontation coming and you were being presented with innocent victims as fodder in the situation, to put it simply, and this was a challenge for the UN.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: We would tender 1322, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P2180, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: Thank you. If we now look to 65 ter document 5229.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: And this is a pair of letters from UNPROFOR containing essentially the same information in both letters addressed to two different people. So firstly, can you tell us whose signature that is?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD McELLIGOTT
utterances.text: Cedric Thornberry signs both letters.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: And if you look at the content, what type of letters are these?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD McELLIGOTT
utterances.text: Again, it a protest letter. It talks about applying regulations concerning confiscation of property and again outside the remit of the Vance Plan.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: And why was confiscation of property outside the remit of the Vance Plan?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD McELLIGOTT
utterances.text: Well, the local authorities ... The -- the -- it was -- I'll just read the letter for a moment here, yeah. It's -- again, I think it's referring to the confiscation of property of refugees are taken. And that any action already taken are reversed, so it's the seizure of refugee property.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: And from your own experience, why would that be outside -- you said, the remit of the Vance Plan? What did you mean by that?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD McELLIGOTT
utterances.text: You're back to the basic rights of people again of -- to preserve their life, their property, their home, and this was just seizure of it. Again the consequences of it was that these people were left nothing but the clothing they carried on their back when they were leaving the place.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: We tender 5229, at this stage.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Gosnell.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Mr. President, we would object to the admission of this document through this witness. As Your Honours know we would object to the -- we disagree with the assertions being put forward in the letter, and given its significance, we suggest that this letter should only be tendered with someone who can actually speak to the reasons why these allegations were made so that we can then test that on cross-examination. As it stands, there's no way to test through cross-examination the -- the specific characterisation of the regulations being applied as depriving those who were leaving of their property. And we say that that deprives this document of -- of foundation for admission through this witness. Given that that's the reason why it's being admitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: A quick response, Your Honours. In the witness's statement, there is reference to protest letters sent by Thornberry and he explains why this was done. Now the document is largely self-authenticating. If you look at its format it's quite clear, but he has provided additional information and he has put it into the context of the Vance Plan, which is also described in his statement. So there is sufficient information if the Defence wants to explore that on cross-examination, but we would say irrespective of that, there is a foundation for admission into evidence of this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Overruled. The document is admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P2181, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thanks.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: If we could now look to document 5389. And while that's coming up, while you're getting there, I note at paragraph 151 of your statement you describe a document, which is 5392, that refers to pressure on the RSK to slow down on unification. So my question is: What do they mean by this "unification"? And I'm referring at the moment to, in your statement, where you refer to this "pressure to slow down unification." Before we get to this specific document.

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD McELLIGOTT
utterances.text: May I refer to my statement just to ...

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: Absolutely, yes. Of course. That's para 151 of your statement. So, to repeat my question, what is meant by this "pressure on the RSK to slow down on unification"?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD McELLIGOTT
utterances.text: This, as I understand it, is that they were looking towards the east to perhaps join in with the - what do you call it - Serbia as an approach to where they were going.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: If we now look back to 5389. And apologies for all the shuffling of paper here. Now, this memorandum also discusses unification, this term. And for e-court, could we go to the following page of this document. Now, if we look at the bottom of the document, there's a heading: Humanitarian issues. And it refers to: "CIVPOL reporting many incidents of harassment and intimidation to the militia but in most cases no action has been taken." In which way would UN CIVPOL typically report that information to the militia?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD McELLIGOTT
utterances.text: They would go to -- they -- we had a CIVPOL station at all locations where there were police -- normal police stations with responsibility for enforcing law. And our monitors, or the station commander, would go to the station to meet with them and to bring matters to their notice. In reality, the local police should be advising our people of reports they have as well. But facts on the ground would show that our monitors were picking up information, perhaps, that the local police may never have picked up. So they would go out and meet them and give them the details.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: And the report states that the local militia usually didn't react. How does that fit with your experience in -- during your period of service with UN CIVPOL?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD McELLIGOTT
utterances.text: It goes back again to what I said at an early stage. There tended to be a switching on and switching off of assistance, and you can see that in reports where you will see we're coming to, co-operation is good, then co-operation is waning. Very often, as is mentioned earlier, it can be down to individuals who are present and who are helpful. And that's the environment you had, and that was the way you met the situation. You could get help today and you mightn't get it tomorrow, or you could have it for six weeks and it would go again. So that was a switch on/switch off scenario, and that is reflected in many reports.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: If we look to the second-last paragraph on that page, it refers to meetings between representatives of the Republic of Croatia and RSK local authorities in Geneva. Are you aware of such meetings?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD McELLIGOTT
utterances.text: I am. I did attend a number of them, but I wasn't -- that was the front stage on it. I was there as an observer, I would say, in relation to any matters arising in respect of a policing issue. And that could be in relation to planning of events that might emerge from negotiations.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: Your Honours, we tender 5389. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P2182, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: Thank you. Could we now go to 5367. And if we go to the second page of this.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: Firstly, I note that it's from Cedric Thornberry. Is that his signature?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD McELLIGOTT
utterances.text: Yeah -- no, it's not. No. I don't think so. No.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: And if you look to the content of the letter, what type of letter is this?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD McELLIGOTT
utterances.text: Again, it's a letter of protest, raising a -- concerns about the destruction of Catholic churches in Sector East.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: Are you aware of the destruction of Catholic churches in Sector East?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD McELLIGOTT
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: Now, in those situations, did the local militia investigate the destruction of Catholic churches?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD McELLIGOTT
utterances.text: There would be specific reports on that churches, indicating what action was taken, so I would need to -- to look at those, or consult those, if necessary. But there will be -- on the issue of reporting the incident, there will be a reference to what action is being taken.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: Your Honours, we tender 5367.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P2183, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: Now, Mr. McElligott, in your work with UN CIVPOL, were the UN CIVPOL monitors and staff able to undertake measures that had an impact on the numbers of crimes being committed in the UNPAs and pink zones?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD McELLIGOTT
utterances.text: Yes, I believe they did. A significant impact, despite the fact that we were only 633 monitors. We engaged very openly with the community. Our approach was one of community policing, where we got into the community, engaged with the people, and became part of the society there. Our monitors lived in the community. They were unarmed. And they shared whatever social conditions they had with them. And they did that in respect of both the minority Croatian population and, indeed, the Serbian population. So that there was a pretty even-handed approach on their part. And I think if you look at the Benkovac situation, when the Serbian people fled from the scene, their first port of call was CIVPOL. So that shows that they had made a mark with them.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: What types of measures are you aware of UN CIVPOL monitors using to try and affect the crimes occurring -- Apologies. I'll repeat. What types of measure specifically are you aware of UN CIVPOL and its monitors taking to address the crimes being committed in the areas that it was operating in?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD McELLIGOTT
utterances.text: There are two specifically referred to in this document. One was in Sector South where the co-ordinator -- the director of civil affairs, Viktor Andreev, and the CIVPOL monitors came together with an initiative to establish patrols, including night patrols in the communities to protect them. Sector North is a significant one allowed from the CIVPOL sector commander where he actually sought for a substantial logistical support to base himself in the minority communities with, I suppose, a mobile type of response office to deal with hot spots as they arose. And you have day-to-day patrolling and, indeed, night patrols. One in Sector South again where they linked up with the Canadian -- not the Canadian but the Kenyan Battalion in carrying out joint patrols. And, again, I think the approach in linking up and taking that approach was one of spreading your resources as best you could, that you had CIVPOL and the military able to -- maybe to get five patrols or six patrols instead of two by having a CIVPOL monitor in each vehicle, and perhaps a Kenyan soldier as well. So those type of initiatives were taken. They were responding to the needs. And, as I said, we had only 630 people. The people with responsibility for the task, as I have said earlier, had 7.000, and if they made any effort, I think they would have made a significant difference to that -- those communities.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: I see the time, Your Honours. I just note about the video that we discussed earlier, which was 4848.1, so it is from TV Serbia, TV Belgrade, and it's a news programme, News 2, that was it was being reported by. And, as I said, our main purpose with producing that and wanting it admitted is the fact that it was publicly broadcast. And we have a date in October 1992 for the approximate date of that video. That's the clip with Jeannie Peterson that the witness described.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Would that change your -- would this information change your objection, Mr. Gosnell?

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: No, it doesn't, Mr. President. And, in fact, I would add the objection. I don't understand the purpose of tendering it. We've now heard -- because we've now heard two different explanations from the Prosecution as the purpose. At the beginning, they said the purpose was in order to have this witness provide additional information as to what Jeannie Peterson meant, and now apparently the only purpose is to indicate that it was publicly broadcast. And we have the witness's commentary. If Jeannie Peterson's views are later tendered in proper form, then this witness's commentary can be viewed in light of that. But this is -- the objection is -- is maintained and, in fact, added to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: I do think that we have everything we need on the record, Mr. Gillett.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: Okay. Just to clarify, though, we were tendering it for three purposes, in fact. The purpose that it corroborates Mr. McElligott's statement, because he does refer to Jeannie Peterson. And it shows that she was involved in these activities, quite clearly. It refers to topics, and we believe that his comments amplify those topics and provide further information. And, thirdly, it's the fact that it was publicly broadcast. So these were the reasons that we were tendering the document. That is the [Overlapping speakers] ... to clarify because maybe I wasn't clear earlier about that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: And, in your view, is there anything -- anything with regard to these three reasons that is not on the record -- that is not on the record now?

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: The -- the visual images we sometimes find useful in terms of the clip shows how people were present. The number of reporters with cameras, et cetera. And in terms of these messages being publicly broadcast, we do consider that relevant, and it -- now it's on the record from me, but it's -- it's -- in the video, it's much clearer than me trying to explain that, or even the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: The objection is still sustained. Mr. McElligott, we finish here our -- our hearing for today. We expect you to be back in the courtroom tomorrow morning at 9.00, which means that you are not released as a witness, implementing that you cannot discuss your testimony with anybody for the moment, and you cannot talk to any of the parties. The court usher will escort you out of the courtroom. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Court adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Thursday, the 20th day of June, 2013, at 9.00 a.m.
